t: The stairway, cut from the passage itself
ref: “A House in Memory” — cut-up word strips arranged into the shape of a house
mech: Words cut from a book and physically arranged into the outline of the thing the book is about. Form and content are the same object.
ours: Every word of Genesis 28 cut into paper strips and laid as a staircase rising off the bottom-left corner — each step a phrase, treads shortening as they climb, some strips upside down. Real scissors, real shadows, photographed flat. The text becomes the ladder.
where: Cover candidate, or the poster page

ref: Nike, “JUST ___ IT” — two enormous words holding the corners, the whole story crammed inside at body size
mech: You read the shout, then discover the whisper. The display type is the container, not the message.
ours: Those four words at poster scale. Inside the letters, at 9pt, every place in scripture God says it — to Jacob at Bethel, Moses at the bush, Joshua, Gideon hiding in a winepress, Jeremiah who says he is too young, the disciples at the very end of Matthew. Dozens of instances filling the negative space.

t: The stone, and everything it was called
ref: “One man's trash / another's treasure” — hundreds of handwritten opinions radiating from one photographed object
mech: The noise around the object is the argument. Nothing is stated; the density states it.
ours: An ordinary rock photographed dead centre. Radiating outward in handwriting, everything it was called: worthless · in the way · just a rock · not worth carrying · a pillow · a pillar · Bethel · the house of God. Dismissive nearest the stone; true at the edges.

t: What to say when somebody is grieving
ref: “Alternatives to How are you?” — a hand-lettered grid replacing one useless question with thirty-five usable ones
mech: Immediately practical. You could use it in the next hour.
ours: A grid of things that actually help — and, the part nobody prints, a shaded row of what not to say. “Everything happens for a reason” is not in the Bible. Job's friends got it wrong for thirty chapters and the book records every word so we would know. The closest thing to right is the seven days they said nothing.

ref: “12 most beautiful questions ever asked” — a plain numbered list, no design at all
mech: The typography is nothing. The selection is everything. People screenshot it because every line lands.
ours: He asks about 300 questions and answers almost none of them. Set them plainly, numbered, with references and no commentary. The absence of answers is the design.

t: To the ones who were not chosen
ref: Apple, “To the crazy ones” — a full page of centred, stepped prose, no image
mech: Accumulation. A company spent a full page saying something that was not about its product.
ours: A full page listing the people God picked, each one disqualified on paper. The youngest son out in the field. The murderer. The prostitute. The tax collector. The one who denied him three times. Stepped and ragged, ending on the turn: these are the ones he picked on purpose.

ref: “300 Positive Words of Encouragement” — hundreds of single words in tiny columns
mech: You do not read it, you scan until one hits you. Density does the work.
ours: Every name scripture gives a person, in columns, each with its reference set tiny: chosen · kept · named · found · carried · known · called · redeemed · adopted · not forgotten · engraved on his palms. Hundreds. Somewhere in that wall is the one you needed today.

ref: The design-thinking squiggle — one continuous line, a knot that gradually becomes straight
mech: No words needed. Everyone recognises their own life in it.
ours: The same line, labelled at four points: Beersheba at the tangled start · the stone in the middle of the knot · Bethel where it begins to straighten · twenty years along the straight part. Caption: most of this drawing is the part nobody writes down.

ref: The Porch Light Theory · the highlighted letter · the piano page — handwriting with highlighter, circling and blackout over it
mech: Handwriting makes it feel like it was meant for you. The highlighter shows you someone else's emphasis. The object underneath grounds it.
ours: Someone's real handwriting — doubting, stressed — with six places where a single word is crossed out or circled and an arrow runs to the correction, verse written out in the margin in red. “I'll come back when I've got it together” → circled. “I'm too far gone” → cross out too far, margin note: he RAN. A plain rock, cut out on white, sits below it.

t: What else was in the room
ref: Microsoft “We see” · the fence photograph · the kitchen illustration — a real photo with hand-drawn line art continuing out of it
mech: The drawing shows what is not visible in the frame. Photograph and drawing argue with each other.
ours: Photograph an ordinary place — a stairwell, a kitchen at 11:40pm, a car park. Draw over it in one continuous white line what the text says is also present: the ramp, the traffic going both directions. Caption: the photograph is real. So is the other thing.

t: The half of the conversation you can hear
ref: Cleveland Institute of Art, “Please fill in the blanks” — highlighted redaction used as a form
mech: The answers are redacted and the questions sit underneath. You read the shape of a conversation you cannot hear.
ours: Prayers with the human half printed and God's half redacted to blocks — then, at the bottom, one block left unredacted. The argument: you are not owed the whole transcript, and one line is enough to go on.

ref: “Three-word quotes” — a list where the constraint is the format
mech: Short enough that every entry is memorable. The format is the argument.
ours: The shortest verses in the Bible, set enormous, one per line, references tiny. The page argues that it does not take many words.

ref: Weekly Bingo for tiny achievements · January's Inner Work — a hand-drawn grid you circle
mech: Things too small to count as achievements, which is exactly why ticking them feels good. It becomes yours the moment you mark it.
ours: Twenty-five squares of ordinary faithfulness nobody claps for: told the truth when a lie was easier · let someone go first · said sorry first · didn't say the thing · read one verse · sat with somebody who was sad · asked for help. Free square in the middle: you woke up.

t: How to pray when you don't know what to say
ref: “How to journal when you don't know what to say” — a bulleted list that removes the excuse
mech: Every bullet lowers the bar rather than raising it.
ours: Same structure, same generosity, every line sourced. Start with a complaint — Psalm 13 does. Say you don't believe and ask for help with that. Use somebody else's words; the Psalms are borrowed prayers. Say nothing — Romans 8:26 says the Spirit does it for you. Be angry out loud; Job never apologises for it.

ref: “In my control / out of my control” — one hand-drawn irregular loop
mech: Inside the loop, what is yours. Outside, everything else. The wobble in the line makes it human.
ours: Inside: today · your next sentence · who you tell · whether you go back. Outside: the outcome · other people · the twenty years · whether it makes sense yet.

ref: Joy Break Generator — three columns you combine
mech: Pick one from A, one from B, one from C. A generator, not a list — it makes the reader do something.
ours: Column A: a place you already are (a car · a kitchen at night · a waiting room). Column B: one verse. Column C: one minute of what (read it out loud · say it back angry · write it on your hand). Any combination is a legitimate start. That is the theology of the page.

ref: The Fixer's Manifesto · Incomplete Manifesto for Growth · Nike's 10 principles · Dieter Rams
mech: Numbered declaratives, no hedging, set as a wall of type. Reads like something pinned above a workbench.
ours: Twelve numbered lines, each a verse in plain speech with the reference set small. 1. NOTHING IS DISQUALIFYING. 2. YOU DO NOT HAVE TO FIX YOURSELF FIRST. 3. SMALL IS NOT NOTHING. 4. DOUBT IS ALLOWED IN THE ROOM.
where: Back of the book, or inside front

t: What people said in the dark
ref: “Banksy said / Matisse said” — a hand-lettered grid, one person per cell
mech: Democratic. No quote is bigger than another.
ours: Each cell one line from someone at their lowest, with the reference. Job said the day I was born should be erased. David said how long must I wrestle with my thoughts. Elijah said I have had enough, take my life. Jeremiah said I am mocked all day long. Jesus said my God, why have you abandoned me. Nothing resolved on the page.

ref: “Be a Lifeboat” — one hand-drawn object with labels radiating to every function it serves
mech: Warm, homemade, generous. Turns an object into a job description.
ours: One drawn rock with lines out to everything it was: somewhere to put your head · proof you were there · a marker · the thing that got poured on · the start of a house.

ref: “Note to self: FANTASY = a goal without a deadline” — stacked equations, each adding one highlighted term
mech: You watch a thing become another thing by accumulation.
ours: BELIEF = agreeing it is true. FAITH = belief + acting like it. TRUST = faith + time. HOPE = trust + a promise you did not make yourself. Each term in a different highlighter, each with its reference.

t: Take one, leave one, give one away
ref: “Notes to Strangers” — a wall of envelopes you take one from
mech: Physical, anonymous, one-to-one. It works because you did not earn it and nobody watched you take it.
ours: Twelve small perforated notes down a page, each one line and a reference, blank on the back. The paper becomes something that leaves the paper.
where: Near the Spine, so it tears out cleanly

ref: “Perspective Matters” — three drawings of one object from different angles, all labelled the same word
mech: The whole argument is made without a sentence.
ours: The identical scene drawn three times: what Jacob saw (a field, a rock, the dark) · what the people of Luz saw (nothing; an ordinary Tuesday) · what was actually there (the ramp, the traffic, all night). All three labelled BETHEL.

t: Rules for reading the Bible without getting it wrong
ref: The “razors” series — Occam's, Hanlon's, Hofstadter's: one bold rule, one plain example, one small drawing
mech: Consistent template, endlessly repeatable, genuinely useful.
ours: Six of them, same template. Read the sentence before it. If it is a promise, check who it was said to. The Bible reports things it does not approve of. A verse is not a fortune cookie. If it makes you feel superior, re-read it. When in doubt, read it out loud to somebody. This is the one framework format that earns its place, because it protects the reader from us.

ref: The monthly log page — INSPIRED BY / WATCHING / READING / GRATEFUL FOR, ruled and hand-filled
mech: A form you complete by hand. It becomes a record the moment you write on it.
ours: Reading · Carrying · Grateful for · Praying the same thing about · Nobody knows that I · Coming back to. Rules to write on. The last line pre-filled: still here.

ref: Blackout poetry — a page destroyed until a new sentence surfaces
mech: It only works if the words are genuinely there in that order. Otherwise it is white text on bars.
ours: Verified, not faked. I searched eleven books. Three lines are extractable with a tight span: “nothing can separate us from the love of God” (Romans 8:38–39, 65 words) · “you are not alone / I am with you” (John 16:29–33, 73 words — this is the issue title) · “come to me and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28, 18 words). Your line — falling in love with Jesus is the best thing I've ever done — is NOT extractable: the only hit spans 5,382 words across John 11–17. It can still be the ad; it just cannot claim the Bible as its source text.

t: A person made entirely of text
ref: #91 — a portrait collaged from strips of a biography, the figure cut out of the words that describe him
mech: The person and the account of the person are the same material. You cannot look at the man without reading about him.
ours: A human silhouette assembled from strips of Psalm 139 — every strip a phrase about being known, seen, formed, counted. The figure is cut out of the text and stands on a plain road. Nothing drawn; everything cut.
where: A full page, or a Spine cover

t: 20 sentences people think are in the Bible
ref: #94 — “20 Sentences In 60 Seconds That Will Change Your Life”, highlighter over printed lines
mech: A numbered list with a promise of speed, marked up in yellow so it reads like somebody already studied it for you.
ours: Twenty sentences, fifteen genuinely in the Bible and five that absolutely are not — “God helps those who help themselves”, “God won't give you more than you can handle”, “money is the root of all evil”. The five fakes highlighted in a different colour and corrected in the margin. This page makes us trustworthy by admitting what gets misquoted, including by us.

ref: #97 — fixed vs growth mindset drawn as the identical four puzzle pieces, once locked shut and once open
mech: One object drawn twice, with only one property changed. The whole argument is in the difference, and no sentence is needed.
ours: The identical rock drawn twice, same size, same shading. Labelled A PILLOW and A PILLAR. Nothing about the stone changed between the two drawings — only the night in between, and what he did with it in the morning.

ref: #102 — a postbox on a wall beside a rack of tear-off cards: leave your impression behind, drop the card in
mech: Two actions, not one. You take something AND you give something back, anonymously, and the wall keeps both.
ours: Stronger than the tear-off page on its own. A perforated strip of notes to take, and directly beside it a card to fill in and post back — the address printed on it. What comes back becomes page 28 of the next issue. The paper stops being a broadcast.
where: Its own page, near the Spine

ref: #103 — The Creative Manifesto: hand-lettered centred lines inside a thick wobbling blue border
mech: The wobble is the whole personality. A straight frame would make it corporate; the hand-drawn one makes it a gift.
ours: Same treatment for the twelve-line Between Sundays manifesto — hand-lettered, centred, inside a wobbling border in one of our inks. Every line is a verse in plain speech with its reference set tiny underneath. It is designed to be torn out and stuck on a wall.
